title: Architecture and Judgement
premise: Every other course in this block teaches you to build one thing well. None of them ever asks whether you should have built it at all. This one does nothing else. A customer says 'can AI do this' and the valuable answer is frequently 'you do not need AI for this, you need a rule and a lookup table' — and being the person who says that, with numbers, is worth more than being the person who can wire up any architecture on request.
why_here: Placed third, after evaluation, because the comparison it demands is only honest if you can measure. Placed before retrieval, agents and speech, because it frames all three: each of those courses teaches a technique, and this one teaches when the technique is the wrong answer.
laboratory: Career Side Quests has a clean classification problem hiding in it — given a line from a job posting, is it a requirement or is it boilerplate? You can label it yourself in an afternoon, a regular expression will do embarrassingly well on it, and it is currently done by an LLM. That is the whole course in one example.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.bias_warning: The judges are language models being asked to assess arguments about whether a language model was necessary. They are instructed explicitly that a submission concluding 'no LLM needed' is not thereby weaker, and that the criterion is the quality of the comparison rather than the fashionability of the answer.

items.title: An end-to-end classification project
items.locator: The end-to-end project chapter and the classification chapter.

items.title: Choosing what to build

items.title: Three ways to the same answer
items.brief: Take the requirement-versus-boilerplate classification inside Career Side Quests. Label at least 200 lines yourself. Then solve it three ways: a regular expression or keyword rule, a classical classifier over TF-IDF features, and the LLM you currently use. Measure all three on the same held-out split for accuracy, cost per thousand lines, and latency. Report which you would ship and why. The regular expression will do better than you expect, and noticing that is the point of the course.
checkpoints: 200+ lines labelled with a held-out split
accuracy, cost and latency reported for each

modules.title: Metrics that make the decision honest

items.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
items.brief: Abstention as a first-class option — a model permitted to say it does not know.

items.title: Precision, recall, and what each error costs
items.brief: For your M1.4 classifiers, produce confusion matrices and precision-recall curves. Then do the part everyone skips: assign a cost to a false positive and a false negative in this specific product, in whatever unit is real — user trust, wasted review time, a wrong assessment shown to someone. Pick the operating point from that cost, not from the F1 maximum, and say how the choice changes if the costs are reversed.
checkpoints: confusion matrices and PR curves produced

items.title: Is your confidence a probability?
items.brief: Plot a reliability curve for whichever of your three approaches emits a score. If the LLM's stated confidence is not calibrated — it very likely is not — show that, because the next module routes on exactly that number.

items.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction
items.brief: The principled way to attach a guarantee to a threshold. Read at least through the classification section; the whole paper is worth it if the maths lands.

items.title: Human-in-the-loop and continual learning
items.locator: The sections on human-in-the-loop review and on feedback loops from production.

items.title: Set the threshold from data
items.brief: Design a routing policy for your classifier: above a confidence threshold it acts automatically, below it a human reviews. Set the threshold from your calibration work and the error costs from M2.4, not by feel. Report the resulting automation rate, the expected error rate among auto-actioned cases, and the human review load per thousand items. Then state the threshold at which the human becomes the bottleneck.
checkpoints: policy defined with a derived threshold
automation rate and residual error reported

items.title: The escalation policy
items.brief: Write what the reviewing human actually sees, what they are asked to decide, and what happens to their decision afterwards. A review queue that does not feed back into the system is a cost centre, not a loop. Include what happens when the human disagrees with the model repeatedly.

items.title: Retention: confidence routing and review design
Model selection and build-versus-buy
items.locator: The chapters on choosing a model and on the build-versus-buy decision.

items.title: Models overview
items.optional_reason: The same page is required reading in AIE-101 M1.3, two courses earlier. Re-read only if the capability columns of your matrix feel guessed.

items.title: A model selection matrix
items.brief: Build the matrix you would actually hand a customer: candidate models down one axis, and intelligence, latency, cost, context length, structured output, tool calling, multimodal support and reliability across the other. Populate the cells from your own measurements where you have them and cite the source where you do not. Then apply it to two of your own features and show it producing different answers for each.

items.title: Build, buy, or call an API
items.brief: For one capability in your products, cost four routes over three years: call a frontier API, self-host an open model, fine-tune a small model, or build conventional software with no model at all. Include the costs people leave out — engineering time, on-call, model deprecation, migration when a provider changes terms. State the volume at which the answer changes.

items.title: Retention: model selection and total cost
Route it
items.brief: Ship a hybrid path in one of your live products: a cheap deterministic or classical component handling the cases it handles well, an LLM handling the rest, and a confidence-based route to human review where neither is trusted. The measurement from M1.4 must be visible in the design — if the LLM handles everything, the report has to show why the cheaper components lost.
checkpoints: each branch justified by a measurement

items.title: The architecture decision record
items.brief: Write the decision record: the problem, the options considered, what each measured, the choice, the cost, and the conditions under which you would revisit it. One page. This is the document that gets you taken seriously in a technical review, and almost nobody writes it.

items.title: Publish
items.brief: Publish as the next chapter of your public engineering log. This chapter is the one most likely to be read by a hiring manager, because it is the only one that argues against using the technology they are hiring for.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your report at defense time, answered aloud without notes.
sample_question_shapes: A customer wants an LLM for something a rule would solve. Talk me out of your own product.
Your threshold auto-actions 80% of cases. Describe the user harmed by the 20% that slips through.
Which cell in your selection matrix are you least confident about, and what would you measure to fix it?

machine_checks.check: 200 or more hand-labelled lines with a held-out split declared before modelling
all three approaches evaluated on the identical split
cost and latency reported alongside accuracy

criteria.criterion: The rule baseline is built in good faith

levels.0: A token regex built to lose.
levels.3: Genuinely the best rule the author could write, with the iterations shown.
Follows the numbers including where they contradict what the author shipped, and says so.

criteria.criterion: Cost and latency are weighed, not just accuracy

levels.3: Weighed at a stated volume, with the accuracy-per-dollar trade made explicit.

rubrics.anti_gaming: A strawman rule baseline invalidates the entire course. Judges are instructed to inspect the rule and to score criterion 1 at 0 where it is a single naive pattern, regardless of how good the rest of the submission is.

machine_checks.check: confusion matrix and precision-recall curve produced per approach
an explicit cost assigned to each error type

levels.3: Assigned in a real unit with who bears the cost named.

criteria.criterion: The operating point follows the cost

levels.3: Cost-derived, with the reversed-cost case worked through.
Plotted, with the miscalibration quantified and its direction stated.

machine_checks.check: threshold derived from calibration and error costs, not chosen by inspection
automation rate, residual error rate and review load all reported

levels.3: Derived with the guarantee it does and does not provide stated plainly.
Quantified against a realistic reviewer throughput, with what happens when volume doubles.

criteria.criterion: The reviewer's task is designed, not assumed

levels.3: Specified down to what is shown, what is asked, and how long it should take.
Fed back with the persistent-disagreement case handled explicitly.
Sourced, with the author's own measurements distinguished from published claims.
Different answers per feature, with the deciding attribute named in each case.
Includes on-call, deprecation and migration, each with a number or a stated assumption.
Derived with the arithmetic shown.

machine_checks.check: at least two branches, one of which is not an LLM call

criteria.criterion: Each branch is justified by a measurement

levels.3: Every branch traceable to a specific result from M1.4 or M2.4.
Functional, and a low-confidence case demonstrably reaches it end to end.
Argued at their strongest, including the one the author nearly chose.
Stated as observable triggers a colleague could monitor for.

machine_checks.check: published at the same origin as previous chapters, reachable from the log index

criteria.criterion: The argument survives a sceptical reader

levels.3: Evidenced such that a reader who disagrees can check the claim themselves.

criteria.criterion: Connects to the body of work

levels.0: Standalone post with no relation to earlier chapters.
levels.1: Links to an earlier chapter without using it.
levels.3: Builds on an earlier result and revises or qualifies it in light of what this course found.

criteria.criterion: Willing to argue against the technology

levels.3: Makes the case against their own architecture better than the questioner does.
Describes a specific person harmed by the automation rate they chose.
Names one and says what would firm it up.

rubrics.integrity: Assessed from the recording and transcript. Long pauses are not penalised; reading from a prepared text is.

completion.required: All assignments and the project submitted. Readings are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the three architecture skills and on classical model evaluation. FSRS then decays them.
